summary: Specifies the Discard service, which throws away any data it receives. It is an Internet Standard for hosts that choose to implement it.

plainLanguage.summary: This document defines a service that accepts network data and quietly throws it all away, answering nothing. It is a simple tool for testing and measuring a network path.

subtitle: A small service that silently throws away whatever it receives, used for debugging and measurement.

tldr.problem: Network engineers need a very simple place to send data that will accept it and do nothing with it, for debugging and measuring.
tldr.mechanism: A discard service throws away any data it receives and sends no response, listening on port 9 over either TCP or UDP.
tldr.outcome: Hosts that choose to implement a Discard Protocol are expected to follow this standard, and implementing it is optional.

today: RFC 863 is an Internet Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What a Discard Service Is
sections.content:
The RFC introduces the discard service as a useful debugging and measurement tool, and describes it in one line: it simply throws away any data it receives.

Hosts on the ARPA Internet that choose to implement a Discard Protocol are expected to adopt and implement this standard.
sections.plainLanguage: You send it data and it never sends anything back. That makes it handy for testing.

sections.title: TCP and UDP Discard
sections.content:
The TCP-based discard service is a connection based application. A server listens for TCP connections on TCP port 9. Once a connection is established, any data received is thrown away and no response is sent. This continues until the calling user terminates the connection.

The UDP-based discard service is a datagram based application. A server listens for UDP datagrams on UDP port 9. When a datagram is received, it is thrown away and no response is sent.
sections.plainLanguage: Over a connection it keeps listening until you close it, and stays silent. For single messages it takes each one and drops it, also silently.

sections.title: Standard Status
sections.content: RFC 863 is an Internet Standard from May 1983. The text defines only the two port 9 behaviors described above, and offers no other detail.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a listener that never answers: whatever is sent to it simply disappears.
